goal.what: The developers see, before anyone writes a body, whether the parts that the parts' design draws fit together, and whoever decided the parts' design mends each place where they don't.

critical_success_factors.what: Each decision that the design gives a part has one place in the code.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each module state at its top the one decision that it alone hides, and does each decision that the design gives a part lie in exactly one module?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who builds or changes a part finds the one module that holds each decision, and a decision split across modules shows a part that the design cut wrong while nothing is built on it yet. David Parnas's [information hiding](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623) divides a system into modules by the decisions likely to change, each hidden in one module, and arc42's [building block view](https://docs.arc42.org/section-5/) at level 2 opens each component of level 1 into its blocks in this way.

items.text: Read the parts' design, from the decisions agreed for it and what the repository already holds: what each part decides, the kinds of data, each step of each use, where each part's files lie, and the language and the tools.

List, for each part, each decision that the design gives it: each choice its job says it makes, each step it takes in a use, and each kind of data that only it reads or writes, such as the layout of a file that it keeps.

Give each decision to one module, and ask of each pair of decisions in a part whether one could change while the other stays, such as a file's layout and the rules that read it. Where one could, give each a module of its own, and where a change of one always changes the other, keep them in one module.

Make each module's file where the design places its part, in the language that the design names, and write at its top the sentence that the note of Module opening in the template asks for, naming the decision, not the steps, such as `The layout of a record on disk.` Make too each other file that the design places and the parts read, such as a manifest or a setting, in its form, and have each command's entry call its interface, so that a case reaches each empty body.

Once each module states its decision, take a change that the users might come to ask for, such as a new field in what a part keeps, read only the modules' first sentences, and name the one module to open. Where you name none or more than one, move the decision or rewrite the sentence, or, where the design itself places the decision in two parts, list it as a gap as N4 says, until the change names one module.

critical_success_factors.what: Each handoff between the parts has an interface that both sides build to.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each handoff that reaches a part have an interface that states what it takes, what it gives, and each way it refuses, with its body left empty?
necessary_conditions.why: Developers who build the two sides of a handoff apart build to one contract, and a body left empty keeps the skeleton about how the parts fit, not how each works. Bertrand Meyer's [design by contract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_by_contract) states each routine by what it requires, what it ensures, and what it refuses.

items.text: For each use, take each handoff that reaches a part, and name the module whose decision answers it. That module offers an interface that carries the handoff, and handoffs that take one form, such as each event of one kind from a host, may share one interface that names each of them in its contract. For each handoff that a part sends to something outside the product, such as a command of the host, the module that sends it offers an interface that carries it, so that a test can put a double in its place. A module that no handoff reaches offers only what the other modules of its part call, and a part offers only what a handoff reaches, since a name that nothing calls is a part that no use needs.

For each interface, write its contract from the use and the kinds of data: what it takes, as the kind of data handed in; what it gives, as the kind of data handed back or on to the next part; what else it changes, such as a file it writes; and each way it refuses, from each branch of the use that stops or sends work back.

Write each interface in its module with the types it takes and gives, such as in its signature where the language allows, and its contract beside it, such as in its doc comment, with its body left so that a call fails and names the interface, such as one that raises `NotImplementedError('answers.due')`, since a failing case then names the part it reached, and empty bodies alike read as copied code to the checks that the agreed testing names.

Follow each use from handoff to handoff, and check that what each interface gives is what the interface of the next handoff takes, such as by a throwaway file that passes each call's result to the next call, run through the type checker that the agreed testing names, since the checker sees a handoff only where code passes a value on. A type that doesn't fit is a gap that N4 lists.

Where the module that a handoff reaches would find again what the module that sends it already found, such as the start that a resume resumes, have the interface give it, since a thing found twice is one decision in two modules, which the type checker passes.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each part that holds a prompt have a file that states when to use the prompt, what it gives, and the form of what it takes and gives, with its steps left empty?
necessary_conditions.why: A prompt is a part whose body an AI carries out, so the parts beside it fit only where its file states, as an interface does, when it runs and the form of what passes in and out.

items.text: For each part that the design gives a prompt as its type, such as a skill or a subagent, take from its uses when it starts, what data it takes, and what data it gives back.

Make its file where the design places it, with its description, which says when to use the prompt and what it gives, and the form of what it takes and gives, such as a JSON Schema, its steps left empty.

critical_success_factors.what: Each place where the design can't be built reaches whoever decided it before anyone builds around it.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the list of gaps name each place where the skeleton can't follow the design, each with the element of the design that it bears on?
necessary_conditions.why: A gap found in the skeleton is mended in the design while nothing rests on it, and a gap that the design mends in the code alone leaves the document wrong for every developer after. SWEBOK v4's Software Design places the detailed design below the architecture, so a design that can't follow the architecture goes back to it.

items.text: Read the skeleton against the design, and list each gap: a decision that no module can hold without another; a module whose first sentence needs `and` for two decisions that change for different reasons; a handoff that no interface can carry, or data on it that the kinds of data lack; a type that doesn't fit across a handoff; and a part that no handoff reaches.

Write each gap in the form that the note of Gaps in the template gives, and leave its place in the skeleton open, holding only the modules, interfaces, and kinds of data that the design draws, since a part invented there hides the gap from whoever decided the parts' design, and the cases then build on it.
Where the design changes, change the skeleton to it as N1 to N3 say, and read it again for gaps, until you list none.
